newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour market still tightening - analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour market still tightening - analysts.

text.p: Britain's labour market is continuing to tighten in spite of a modest fall in unemployment in May and average earnings growth will pick up later in the year, analysts said on Tuesday.
Unemployment dropped to a seven-year low of 5.8 percent of the workforce but that represented only an 18,400 fall in the number of jobless over the month.

The Office for National Statistics said the backlog of claims caused by a switch to a new system -- the Jobseekers Allowance -- which had artificially inflated the fall in unemployment seen in recent months had now petered out.
But James Barty, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said the real trend rate of fall was probably still 30,000 people or more each month.
"Today's numbers come on the back of some very heavy declines. The key point is the market is tightening," he said.
In April for instance, the pool of jobless shrunk by 56,400 people while in January and February more than 60,000 people were taken off the dole queues each month.

"It's possible average earnings could move lower, but later in the year labour market pressures will start to come through and we expect average earnings growth up at five percent by the end of the year," Barty said.
Underlying annual average earnings growth held steady at 4.5 percent in April while actual earnings growth was even lower, at 4.2 percent.

Economists said the effects of large bonuses paid to City employees were fading out of the equation. And the lack of immediate upward pressure on wages would allow Britain's monetary policy committee to think twice before raising interest rates again soon.
Base rates were pushed a quarter-point higher to 6.5 percent last Friday.

"The smaller than expected monthly decline in unemployment should help to allay some fears about the labour market tightening," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc. "Next month, markets will be looking for a decline in average earnings growth to below 4.5 percent.
David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders, said Wednesday's figures only argued for a delay in monetary tightening.

"The trend is for a continued fall in unemployment and if this goes on throughout the year it will exert increasingly upward pressure on wages," he said. "We are seeing a repreive for policy-makers as the need to raise interest rates may have lessened somewhat."
The average earnings data reflect the skewed nature of Britain's economic recovery -- a booming service sector standing in stark contrast to manufacturers hampered by the strength of the pound.
Service sector wages grew an underlying 4.75 percent in the year to April while manufacturing wages were up only 4.25 percent.

Tom Rayner, economist at Societe Generale, said the service sector was the key area -- representing as it does about two-thirds of gross domestic product. "We're still seeing wage pressures here and this will eventually feed through into the underlying series."
Andy Cates, UK economist at UBS, said base rates would have to rise again this year, to 6.75 percent.
"Insofar as average earnings growth has remained unchanged...today's labour market figures reduce the chances of a further base rate rise in the near-term," he said.
"Nevertheless, the prospective strength of domestic demand combined with an uncomfortably strong level of monetary growth means that base rates will still have to rise."
